overview.title: 📖 Overview: The One-Year Clock on a Walled City House
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 31a–31b
overview.hebrewSource: הַמּוֹכֵר בֵּית בְּבָתֵּי עָרֵי חוֹמָה — הֲרֵי זֶה גּוֹאֵל מִיָּד, וְגוֹאֵל כׇּל שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: A new mishna and chapter address a special Torah category: a house within a city walled since the era of Joshua. Unlike an ancestral field, such a house can be redeemed at any time during the year following its sale — but if that year passes unredeemed, it becomes the buyer's forever, never returning even at the Jubilee. The Gemara works out precisely how that year is counted, debates whether repaying the buyer in full (without deducting for his year of residence) constitutes forbidden interest, and contrasts the strict one-year clock on an ordinary sale with the far more permissive rule for redeeming such a house from the Temple treasury. The daf closes with Hillel's practical fix for buyers who hid to run out the clock.

slides.subtitle: A tight one-year window, then permanent loss

House becomes the buyer's forever (חָלוּט) — does not return even at the Jubilee
His son may redeem in his place
Seller redeems from the buyer's son
The original sale date — not from any later resale
Includes an intercalated leap-year month; applies equally to sale and to gift

slides.title: 💰 Repaying in Full: Interest, or Not?
slides.subtitle: The mishna calls it 'like a form of interest, yet not interest' — the Gemara tests that claim

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: A baraita flatly states: this IS full-fledged interest — the Torah simply permitted it as an exception!

lines.speaker: R' Yoḥanan
lines.text: No contradiction: our mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda, that baraita follows the Rabbis — they dispute a related case of a conditional field-sale securing a loan.

lines.speaker: The case
lines.text: If a lender takes a conditional sale of a debtor's field (voided if the loan is repaid on time), the Rabbis permit it only if the SELLER keeps eating the produce meanwhile — if the LENDER eats it, that's 'interest that might apply' (a one-sided uncertainty), forbidden.

lines.speaker: R' Yehuda
lines.text: Even the lender may eat the produce — citing the real case of Baitos ben Zunin, ruled on by Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.

lines.speaker: Rava's alternate framing
lines.text: Actually, all agree 'one-sided possible interest' is forbidden; they truly disagree about interest given on condition it will be refunded if the sale is voided.

slides.title: ⛪ A Consecrated House: Redeemable Forever
slides.subtitle: The Temple treasury doesn't get the buyer's one-year advantage

steps.content: 1️⃣ One who CONSECRATES his walled-city house may redeem it from the Temple treasury at ANY time — no twelve-month deadline at all
2️⃣ Why? 'To the one who bought it... throughout his generations' (Lev. 25:30) — the Temple treasury has no 'generations,' so it can never claim permanent ownership
3️⃣ But if ANOTHER person redeems it FROM the Temple treasury, the ordinary twelve-month clock starts running against that new owner

4️⃣ Rav Safra: the phrase 'it shall not go out in the Jubilee' is needed for the case where the Jubilee falls mid-year of an ordinary sale — the house still becomes the buyer's permanently and does NOT revert early

slides.title: 🚪 Hillel's Takanah: No More Hiding
slides.subtitle: A practical fix for a practical abuse
slides.label: The problem and the fix:
slides.text: Originally, a buyer who wanted the house permanently would simply hide on the final day of the twelve months, making it impossible for the seller to hand over the redemption money in time. Hillel instituted that the seller could instead deposit the money in the Temple treasury's chamber, then break down the door of the house and enter — with the buyer free to collect his money from the chamber whenever he liked.
slides.hebrewSource: הִתְקִין הִלֵּל שֶׁיְּהֵא חוֹלֵשׁ מְעוֹתָיו לַלִּשְׁכָּה, וִיהֵא שׁוֹבֵר אֶת הַדֶּלֶת וְנִכְנָס

slides.title: 🤝 A Halakhic Ripple: Conditional Divorce
slides.subtitle: Rava draws a surprising inference from Hillel's ordinance

steps.content: 1️⃣ Hillel had to invent a workaround so that 'giving against someone's will' would count as valid payment
2️⃣ The Gemara infers: ordinarily, forcing money on someone who refuses it does NOT count as a valid act of giving
3️⃣ Rava applies this to a conditional get: 'this is your bill of divorce on condition you give me 200 dinars' — if she pays willingly, she is divorced
4️⃣ But if she is forced to pay against her will, the condition is not fulfilled and the divorce does NOT take effect

callout.label: Source:
callout.text: מִדְּאִיצְטְרִיךְ לֵיהּ לְהִלֵּל לְתַקּוֹנֵי נְתִינָה בְּעַל כׇּרְחוֹ הָוְיָא נְתִינָה — 'From the fact that Hillel needed to institute that giving against one's will counts as giving...'

summary.principle: A house in a city walled since Joshua's era carries a strict, once-only one-year redemption window after an ordinary sale — after which it is lost forever — but the same house redeemed from the Temple treasury enjoys no such deadline, and Hillel's ordinance ensured a determined seller could always exercise his right even against a buyer trying to run out the clock.

flowSteps.content: 🏘️ Walled-city house: redeemable any time within 12 months of sale, then permanently the buyer's
📅 The year is counted precisely — from the original sale, including leap months, day-to-day and hour-to-hour

columns.content: 💰 Full repayment without deduction resembles interest — permitted by the Torah as an exception, or reframed via a conditional-sale dispute
⛪ Consecrated to the Temple, the same house can be redeemed at any time, with no deadline at all

flowSteps.content: 🚪 Hillel's takanah stops a hiding buyer from running out the clock — deposit the money, break the door, move in
🎓 Key Principle: a Torah-fixed deadline is absolute, but the halakha ensures a determined party can always actually exercise the right the deadline protects

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what happens to a house in a walled city if the seller does not redeem it within twelve months of the sale?
o: It automatically returns to the seller at the next Jubilee Year
It becomes the buyer's property in perpetuity, never returning even at the Jubilee
The sale is voided and the money is refunded
The seller gets an additional twelve months to redeem it
quiz.e: Unlike an ancestral field, a walled-city house becomes the buyer's permanent possession once the twelve-month redemption window closes — critically, it does not revert to the seller even in the Jubilee Year.

quiz.q: Why, according to Rav Safra, does the verse need to add 'it shall not go out in the Jubilee' if the house already becomes the buyer's 'in perpetuity'?
o: Because 'in perpetuity' only applies to gifts, not sales
It addresses a case where the Jubilee Year falls in the middle of the twelve-month redemption period, teaching the house still does not revert early
It teaches that houses can never be sold during the Jubilee Year
It has no independent function and is purely stylistic
quiz.e: Rav Safra explains this phrase is needed specifically for the scenario where the Jubilee arrives during the sale's one-year window, to clarify that the house does not prematurely leave the buyer's possession just because the Jubilee occurred.

quiz.q: How does the halakha for a CONSECRATED walled-city house differ from an ordinary sale of the same kind of house?
o: Both have identical twelve-month deadlines
The owner may redeem a consecrated house from the Temple treasury at any time, with no fixed deadline, since the Temple treasury 'has no generations'
A consecrated house can never be redeemed at all
Only the Temple treasury may initiate redemption, never the original owner
quiz.e: Because the verse specifies the house becomes the buyer's 'throughout his generations,' and the Temple treasury has no generations, it can never claim permanent ownership — so the original owner may redeem it from hekdesh whenever he wishes.

quiz.q: What problem did Hillel's takanah (ordinance) solve?
o: Buyers overpaying for houses in walled cities
Buyers hiding on the final day of the twelve-month period so the seller could not physically hand over the redemption money in time
Sellers refusing to sell their houses at all
Disputes over which cities counted as 'walled since Joshua'
quiz.e: Hillel instituted that a seller could deposit the redemption money in the Temple treasury's chamber and then break into the house, so a buyer could no longer defeat redemption simply by hiding until the deadline passed.

quiz.q: What does Rava infer from Hillel's ordinance about a husband's conditional bill of divorce ('this is your get on condition you give me 200 dinars')?
o: That the get is always valid regardless of how the money is given
That if the wife pays willingly she is divorced, but if forced to pay against her will, the divorce does not take effect
That conditional divorces are never valid under any circumstances
That the husband can never impose monetary conditions on a get
quiz.e: Rava reasons that since Hillel needed a special ordinance to make 'giving against someone's will' count as valid payment for houses, ordinarily forced payment does NOT count as valid giving — so a wife forced to pay the condition against her will is not considered divorced.
